notes.meaning: Jesus tells a story comparing the kingdom of heaven to a landowner who went out at dawn to hire day laborers for his vineyard. The vineyard represents God's people or His church, and the owner pictures God calling people into His service. God actively seeks out workers rather than waiting for people to find Him.

The landowner agreed to pay the workers one denarius, which was the standard, fair wage for a full day of farm work. They accepted this clear agreement and went straight into the vineyard. The coin shows God's faithfulness to reward those who serve Him.

Around nine o'clock in the morning, the owner returned to the town square and saw other men standing around without work. The marketplace was where day laborers waited hoping someone would hire them. These men were waiting for an opportunity rather than being lazy.

The owner told these men to go into the vineyard, promising to pay whatever was right and fair. Unlike the first group, they did not negotiate a price, but simply trusted his fairness. True service begins with trusting God's goodness rather than bargaining for a reward.

The owner went out again at noon and at three in the afternoon, sending more workers into the vineyard on the same terms. Each time, he brought fresh helpers into his harvest before the day ended. God calls people into His kingdom at different stages throughout their lives.

Around five in the afternoon, with only one hour left of the workday, the owner went back and found still more men standing around. He asked them why they had stayed there all day doing nothing. It was very unusual for an employer to hire workers so close to sunset.

The men answered that nobody had hired them, so the owner told them to go into his vineyard too. They had not refused work earlier, but had simply lacked an opportunity until that moment. As soon as the call came, they went right to work without hesitation.

At sunset, the owner told his foreman to call the laborers and pay them their wages. Under God's law in the Old Testament, poor day laborers had to be paid that very evening before dark. The master ordered him to pay the last group first and the earliest group last.

The workers who were hired at the eleventh hour stepped forward and each received a full denarius. The owner gave them a complete day's wage out of pure kindness, even though they had worked only one hour. God gives His blessings out of generous grace rather than human merit.

When the workers hired at dawn came up, they assumed they would receive extra pay because they had worked longer. Instead, each of them received the exact same coin they had agreed to that morning. Their hopes were dashed because they compared themselves to others instead of remembering their contract.

When they received their pay, they began grumbling against the landowner. Instead of being thankful for honest wages, they felt cheated by his kindness toward the latecomers. Envy often turns a good blessing into bitterness.

The complainers protested that the last group worked only one hour, yet were paid the same as those who bore the heavy labor and blazing heat of the day. They felt insulted that the master treated both groups as equals. They treated service in the vineyard as an exhausting burden rather than a privilege.

The owner gently answered their spokesman, reminding him that no injustice had been done. He pointed out that they had agreed to work for one denarius, and that exact amount had been paid in full. God never breaks a promise or treats anyone unfairly.

The owner told the complaining worker to take his wages and go home. He explained that he freely chose to give the last worker the same amount out of his own goodwill. The reason for divine generosity comes entirely from God's heart, not from how much we achieve.

The owner asked if he lacked the right to spend his own money as he pleased, or if they were jealous because he was kind. The phrase about an evil eye was a Jewish saying for an envious, grudging attitude. God has full authority to show mercy to whomever He wishes without answering to human jealousy.

Jesus explains the lesson of the story: those who seem last will be first, and those who seem first will be last. People who come to God late or are looked down upon can receive full honor, while those who boast of their long service lose their joy. God values humble faith far above proud claims of seniority.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The traditional closing words, 'for many are called, but few chosen,' are omitted in modern translations because the earliest Greek manuscripts do not contain them here.

notes.meaning: While walking up the road to Jerusalem, Jesus pulled the twelve disciples away from the crowd to talk privately. He was traveling toward the Passover feast, fully aware that His death was near. He wanted to prepare His closest followers for what was about to happen.

Jesus warned them that the Son of Man would be handed over to the chief priests and religious scholars in Jerusalem. These Jewish leaders would put Him on trial and condemn Him to death. Jesus clearly foreknew the exact steps of the plot against Him.

Jesus added that the religious leaders would turn Him over to the Roman authorities to be mocked, whipped, and nailed to a cross. He also promised that on the third day He would be raised back to life. Even in the shadow of painful execution, Jesus looked forward with total confidence to His resurrection.

The mother of James and John came to Jesus with her two sons and knelt down to ask for a special favor. She was likely Salome, who traveled with and helped support Jesus' ministry. Her request showed honor for His royal power, even though her ambition was misplaced.

When Jesus asked what she wanted, she requested that her two sons sit at His right and left hand in His coming kingdom. The right and left sides of a king were the highest seats of power and honor. The disciples were still expecting an earthly, political empire where they could hold the top government offices.

Jesus told the two brothers that they did not know what they were asking for. He asked if they were able to drink the cup of suffering that lay ahead of Him, and they boldly claimed they could. In the Bible, a cup often pictures deep sorrow or trials given by God.

Jesus told them they would indeed share His suffering, a prophecy fulfilled when James was martyred and John faced exile and persecution. However, Jesus explained that the places of highest honor are not given through favoritism, but are already prepared by the Father. True closeness to Christ requires a willingness to suffer with Him.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early Church writers taught that Jesus spoke here as a humble servant, or that these seats could not be handed out to the brothers while they sought them out of selfish pride.

notes.meaning: When the other ten disciples heard what James and John had done, they were furious with the two brothers. Their anger grew out of jealousy, because each of them secretly wanted those chief seats for himself. Selfish ambition among believers quickly produces rivalry and division.

Jesus called all twelve disciples together to explain how His kingdom differs from the world. He pointed out that earthly rulers boss people around and like to show off their power. In the world, greatness is measured by how many people you control.

Jesus taught that His followers must never lead by bossing others around. Instead, anyone who wants to be great among them must become a servant to the rest. True greatness in God's eyes is shown through humble care for other people.

Jesus went even further, saying that whoever wants first place must be willing to be everyone's slave. A slave held the lowest status and did the dirtiest work without demanding praise. In God's kingdom, the person willing to do the lowliest chores is given the highest honor.

Jesus pointed to His own life as the ultimate pattern of leadership, saying the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve and give His life as a ransom for many. A ransom was the price paid to buy the freedom of a slave or captive. By dying on the cross, Jesus paid the ultimate cost to set people free from sin.

differ.view: Many Baptists understand 'a ransom for many' to mean that Christ died specifically as a substitute for His chosen people, paying the ransom price for the elect.
Methodists teach that Christ died as a ransom for every human being without exception, and understand 'many' to describe the vast multitude of the whole human family.

notes.meaning: As Jesus and His disciples walked out of the city of Jericho, a huge crowd followed Him. Jericho was an important city near the Jordan River that pilgrims passed on their journey to Jerusalem. The crowd followed eagerly to hear His words and watch His miracles.

Two blind men sitting beside the road heard the noise of the crowd and learned that Jesus was walking by. They cried out loudly, calling Him 'Lord, Son of David' and begging for mercy. By using the title Son of David, they showed their belief that Jesus was the promised Messiah.

The people in the crowd ordered the blind men to be quiet, treating their loud cries as an annoying disturbance. Instead of giving up, the two men shouted even louder for the Son of David to show them mercy. Genuine faith keeps praying even when other people try to silence it.

Jesus stopped in His tracks and called the blind men directly to Him. He asked them what they wanted Him to do for them. Jesus already knew their need, but He invited them to ask out loud so their faith could be openly displayed.

The two men answered simply, asking that their eyes might be opened. They did not ask for money or clothes, but for the miracle of physical sight. They trusted completely that Jesus had the divine power to heal their blindness.

Moved with deep pity, Jesus touched their eyes, and their sight came back immediately. As soon as they could see, they began following Him down the road toward Jerusalem. Receiving Christ's mercy naturally inspires a grateful heart to follow Him wherever He leads.
